## Summary

Research confidence is **Moderate**. Some of this break's ideal conditions are confirmed by sources; others rest on limited evidence. It is the class the app computes from the evidence (how well the break's ideal conditions are documented), not a forecast and not a probability.

Main gaps:

- Sources disagree about the best wind direction.
- Sources disagree about the wave size this break works in.
- Sources disagree about the best tide.
- The sources found do not support this break's listed swell period.

Research notes (research_evidence.json):

> Twelve readable sources from ten publishers: Surf-Forecast, Wikipedia (Portuguese), WSL (three posts), WannaSurf, Surfing-Waves, Yeeew, Surf Atlas, Center of Portugal, The Indian Face and BreakFinder. No peer-reviewed or official study of Supertubos was found. Crossref has only sociology and tourism papers on Peniche; one WebSearch for a bathymetry or morphodynamics thesis found nothing. Not readable: penichesurfguide.com (no response) and visitportugal.com (bot-protection page). TIDE CONFLICT (the profile says low_to_mid): mid to high from WSL's 2015 table and WannaSurf; all tides from Center of Portugal. Mid is best for Yeeew ('all tides, but mid usually is best') and BreakFinder; both agree. No source says low tide is best. A profile value of 'mid' (or mid_to_high) would fit the readable evidence better than low_to_mid. Wind: N-NE agrees with the profile's 40. Surf-Forecast and Yeeew give NE; WSL's text and von Rupp give N; Surfing-Waves N/NE/NW; BreakFinder's text N/NE; pt.wikipedia 'works well with north wind'. N/NW (WannaSurf, The Indian Face) and BreakFinder's templated E contradict. Swell direction: SW-W, with WNW from von Rupp and W/NW from BreakFinder. Everything falls within the window. Size: WSL head high to double overhead (6-12 ft), Center of Portugal up to 12 ft and WannaSurf's minimum 3 ft agree. Yeeew's triple overhead top (about 18 ft) is higher. Period: only von Rupp gives a number, an ideal of about 15 s. Seasonality: the profile's autumn-winter season is supported by WSL (fall into winter) and, indirectly, by Surf-Forecast and WannaSurf (summer flat or poor) and Surf Atlas (tame in August, roaring in December). Bathymetry: sandbars that shift (BreakFinder) but are 'reliable' (von Rupp), with offshore canyon and seafloor relief refracting swell (WSL, von Rupp). Dated sources for this sand-bottom break: Surf Atlas 2026, Yeeew 2024, Center of Portugal 2024, WSL 2015-2019. Low-weight sources: The Indian Face (brand blog), and BreakFinder, whose imported summary line contradicts its own text.

## Ideal conditions

Directions are compass degrees the swell or wind comes FROM, ranges clockwise. Heights keep the scale each source states (breaking face, Hawaiian, swell or relative to the surfer); the app's sizes are breaking face heights in feet. Sources are numbered as in [Sources](#sources).

### Swell height

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum suitable | 3–5 ft (1–1.5 m) [S6] · waist-high [S8] · needs some big swells (it is a little sheltered) [S5] (scale not stated) / body-relative | conflicting | S5, S6, S8 | `wave_height_min_ft` 3 ft (breaking face) |
| Ideal range | head-high to double-overhead; source key: wsl-break-breakdown-peniche; 3 m; with period: 15 s; source key: wsl-portuguese-perspective | documented | S3, S5 | no separate setting; working range 3–12 ft |
| Maximum suitable | 12 ft (4 m) [S10] · 10 ft (3 m) or more [S6] · double-overhead (top of the table range) [S3] · triple overhead [S8] (/ body-relative) | conflicting | S3, S6, S8, S10 | `wave_height_max_ft` 12 ft (breaking face) |

Notes:

- **Minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working at 1.0-1.5 m / 3-5 ft (scale not stated) and Yeeew that it gets good from waist-high, while Nic von Rupp (WSL 2018) says it is a little sheltered so it needs some big swells to get in.
  - S6 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 3m+ / 10ft+”
  - S8 (Yeeew!): “Gets good between waist-high and triple overhead.”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “Supertubes is a little bit sheltered, so you do need some big swells to get in there”
- **Ideal range**: WSL's 2015 break table gives head-high to double-overhead (body-relative faces) and Nic von Rupp (WSL 2018) maybe three metres with a 15-second period (scale not stated); the two use different scales and cannot be compared directly.
  - S3 (World Surf League): “Swell Height: Head-high to double-overhead”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “Not too big of a period - maybe three meters, with a 15-second period.”
- **Maximum suitable**: Center of Portugal gives wave size up to 4 m / 12 ft, WannaSurf holds up to 3m+ / 10ft+ and WSL's table tops out at double-overhead, while Yeeew says it gets good up to triple overhead; none states a measurement scale in feet.
  - S10 (Center of Portugal (regional tourism)): “Wave size – up to 4 metres / 12 feet”
  - S6 (WannaSurf): “Swell sizeStarts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 3m+ / 10ft+”
  - S3 (World Surf League): “Swell Height: Head-high to double-overhead”
  - S8 (Yeeew!): “Gets good between waist-high and triple overhead.”

### Seasonality

| Field | Research value | Status | Sources | App model setting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prime months | Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb | documented | S1, S3, S6, S9 | `best_months` Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb, Mar |

Notes:

- **Prime months**: WSL (2015) says the Atlantic energy runs from the fall into winter (read as about September to February), Surf Atlas that it can look tame in August but is roaring by December, and Surf-Forecast and WannaSurf that summer is mostly flat or poor.
  - S3 (World Surf League): “Beginning in the fall and into winter, there is no lack of energy in the Atlantic ocean.”
  - S9 (Surf Atlas): “The barrels at Supertubos can look positively tame if you come in August, for example. Come December, you can rest assured they'll be roaring and overhead.”
  - S1 (Surf-Forecast.com): “although summer tends to be mostly flat”
  - S6 (WannaSurf): “Dont go in the summer the waves stink then.”
- **Secondary season**: No excerpt states a secondary or shoulder season.
- **Swell sources**: WSL (2015) says there is no lack of energy in the Atlantic from the fall into winter, Nic von Rupp that the swell comes out of really deep water, and Surf-Forecast that waves are just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells.
  - S3 (World Surf League): “Beginning in the fall and into winter, there is no lack of energy in the Atlantic ocean.”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “the sandbars are reliable - the swell comes out of really deep water, and the canyon offshore helps refract swells and break them up”
  - S1 (Surf-Forecast.com): “Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells”
- **Wind patterns**: WSL (2015) refers to October's prevailing north/northwesterlies, Nic von Rupp (WSL 2018) says the north winds are the trade winds and usually offshore in the afternoons, and Portuguese Wikipedia says the prevailing NW winds smooth the sea.
  - S3 (World Surf League): “It's best on a north wind, and October's prevailing north/northwesterlies work pretty well.”
  - S5 (World Surf League): “The north winds are our trade winds, so it's usually offshore in the afternoons...more north wind, which is ideal for Supertubes”
  - S2 (Wikipedia): “Os ventos predominantes de NO alisam o mar e prolongam o tempo em que o surfista pode "entubar".”

## Conflicting information

- **Swell height · minimum suitable**: WannaSurf says it starts working at 1.0-1.5 m / 3-5 ft (scale not stated) and Yeeew that it gets good from waist-high, while Nic von Rupp (WSL 2018) says it is a little sheltered so it needs some big swells to get in.
- **Swell height · maximum suitable**: Center of Portugal gives wave size up to 4 m / 12 ft, WannaSurf holds up to 3m+ / 10ft+ and WSL's table tops out at double-overhead, while Yeeew says it gets good up to triple overhead; none states a measurement scale in feet.
- **Swell direction · ideal bearing**: Surf-Forecast and Surfing-Waves say SW is best, while Nic von Rupp (WSL 2018) calls west-northwest ideal and BreakFinder says it works best on a solid W or NW swell.
- **Swell direction · acceptable range**: WSL's table gives southwest to west and WannaSurf NW, W and SW, while Yeeew says a big S, SW or W swell delivers and Center of Portugal southern and western swells, so the sources disagree on whether S or NW swells work.
- **Swell direction · exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it a reasonably exposed break, while Nic von Rupp (WSL 2018) says it is a little bit sheltered so it needs big swells.
- **Wind · offshore**: Surf-Forecast and Yeeew name the northeast, BreakFinder's text N or NE (but its summary line E), WSL's 2015 text and Nic von Rupp north, Surfing-Waves N, NE or NW, and WannaSurf and The Indian Face N or NW.
- **Tide · preferred stage**: WSL's 2015 table and WannaSurf give mid to high tide, Yeeew says it breaks on all tides but mid is usually best, BreakFinder that mid tide gives the best balance, and Center of Portugal low to full; no source says low tide is best.
- **Geography · break type**: WSL calls it a sand-bottom beachbreak and a sandbar with left and right barrels and WannaSurf a sand-bar wave, while Surf-Forecast (templated wording) calls it a beach and reef break.
- **Geography · exposure**: Surf-Forecast calls it reasonably exposed, while Nic von Rupp (WSL 2018) says it is a little bit sheltered.
